findings.claim: 'the 1961 republic referendum which ended South Africa's Commonwealth membership'
findings.truth: The whites-only republic referendum was held on 5 October 1960. South Africa became a republic and left the Commonwealth on 31 May 1961, after withdrawing its application to stay in.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1960 South African republic referendum'; 'South Africa and the Commonwealth of Nations'

findings.claim: 'Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act (1959) created ten Bantustans (homelands)'
findings.truth: The 1959 Act divided the African population into eight 'national units'. Ten homelands existed by the 1970s-80s, but the Act itself recognised eight.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Promotion of Bantu Self-government Act, 1959': 'the African population was divided into eight peoples'

findings.claim: Practice set carries a 4-mark 'Describe two features' question and a 5-mark 'Outline' question.
findings.truth: The non-British depth study is marked out of 40 with four or five questions: a 2-mark Describe, a 10-mark Explain, either one 10-mark source comparison or two 5-mark source questions (always with two sources), and an 18-mark essay. There is no 4-mark 'Describe two features' (that is another board's form) and no 5-mark 'Outline'. Relabelled to a 2-mark Describe and a 10-mark Explain, since a source question needs two sources the bank does not hold.
findings.evidence: spec assessment tables for the non-British depth study, lines 3060-3208

findings.claim: 'Historian Saul Dubow has argued that apartheid was not simply ideological racism but a system with clear economic beneficiaries among white employers and workers'
findings.truth: Dubow is a real historian of apartheid, but this cheap-labour, economic-beneficiaries thesis is the revisionist argument of Harold Wolpe (1972) and Martin Legassick. Dubow's own intervention runs the other way: he resists reducing apartheid to economic function and stresses ideology and state-building. Options: (a) re-attribute the argument to Harold Wolpe, which is verifiable and keeps the teaching point; (b) drop the name and present it as the economic reading of apartheid; (c) keep Dubow, since he does describe apartheid's material beneficiaries. Recommendation: (a).
findings.evidence: Saul Dubow, 'Apartheid 1948-1994' and 'Racial Segregation and the Origins of Apartheid'; Harold Wolpe, 'Capitalism and cheap labour-power in South Africa' (1972)
findings.ruling: Re-attributed to Harold Wolpe (1972) in body and flashcard.

findings.claim: 'Hospital records analysed in 2023 suggest the real toll may have been higher - at least 91 dead and 281 wounded'
findings.truth: The revised figures are at least 91 killed and more than 238 wounded, from research published by Clark and Worger in 2023-24. There is no hospital-records study and no 281 figure. The 91 is right; the wounded figure and the stated provenance are not.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Sharpeville massacre'

findings.claim: Albert Luthuli described as 'President-General of the ANC 1952-1960'
findings.truth: Luthuli was President-General from December 1952 until his death in July 1967. The 1960 banning did not end his office. The Nobel award is also better given as 'the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize', which he received in Oslo in December 1961.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Albert Luthuli'

findings.claim: Fill-in question keyed so the sentence reads 'South Africa belongs to all people who live in it'
findings.truth: The Freedom Charter reads 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white'. The keyed option misquotes the document the same lesson quotes correctly twice. Changing the option to 'all' keeps the answer key valid and the quotation exact.
findings.evidence: Freedom Charter, Kliptown, 26 June 1955; the lesson's own glossary entry

findings.claim: 'Police arrested seventeen people' at Liliesleaf Farm on 11 July 1963
findings.truth: Thirteen people were arrested in the raid: Bernstein, Goldberg, Goldreich, Hepple, Jassat, Kathrada, Mbeki, Mhlaba, Mlangeni, Moolla, Motsoaledi, Sisulu and Wolpe.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rivonia Trial'

findings.claim: 'Eight men stood trial on charges of sabotage'
findings.truth: Ten accused stood trial. Eight were convicted and sentenced to life; Rusty Bernstein was acquitted and James Kantor was discharged during the trial. Eight is the number sentenced, not the number tried.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rivonia Trial'

findings.claim: Mandela's statement from the dock 'lasted over four hours'
findings.truth: The 20 April 1964 speech from the dock lasted about three hours.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rivonia Trial'; 'I Am Prepared to Die'

findings.claim: Walter Sisulu called 'ANC treasurer-general', 'held on Robben Island until 1989'
findings.truth: Sisulu was Secretary-General of the ANC, 1949-1955. He was moved from Robben Island to Pollsmoor Prison in 1982 and released on 15 October 1989. The wrong job title is also the keyed answer in the matching question.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Walter Sisulu': '9th Secretary-General of the African National Congress, 1949-1955'

findings.claim: 'Mandela was placed in "D Block" in a small cell'
findings.truth: D was the lowest prisoner classification group, not a cell block. Mandela was held in a single cell in B Section and was classified in group D, which is why he had one letter and one visit every six months.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Robben Island'; 'Nelson Mandela'

findings.claim: 'The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) recognised the ANC as the legitimate representative of the South African people'
findings.truth: The OAU Liberation Committee recognised both the ANC and the PAC, and the UN General Assembly in 1974 named both as authentic representatives. Naming the ANC as the sole legitimate representative overstates it, and the ANC/PAC distinction is spec content.
findings.evidence: spec content bullet: 'unbanning of the ANC, Pan African Congress and the South African Communist Party'

findings.claim: 'the inquest was reopened in 1997 and found that members of the security police had caused his fatal injuries'
findings.truth: No inquest was reopened. The 1978 inquest found nobody responsible. In 1997 five former security policemen applied to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for amnesty, admitting the assault; the Commission refused them amnesty in 1999. An invented legal proceeding.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Steve Biko'; TRC amnesty decision AC/1999

findings.claim: 'despite the apartheid government's ban on black trade union membership'
findings.truth: Black trade unions were not banned. African workers were excluded from the legal definition of 'employee', so their unions could not register or use the industrial conciliation system, and strikes by African workers were criminal offences. Recognition came after the Wiehahn Commission in 1979. The model answer repeats the error.
findings.evidence: Industrial Conciliation Act; Native Labour (Settlement of Disputes) Act 1953; Wiehahn Commission 1979

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward answers that show this distinction.'
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: 'the Soweto Students' Representative Council had been active before June 1976'
findings.truth: The SSRC was formed in August 1976, after the uprising. The body that called the 16 June march was an action committee formed at a students' meeting on 13 June 1976, three days before.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Soweto uprising'; 'Soweto Students' Representative Council'

findings.claim: Hector Pieterson described as 'the first victim of the Soweto Uprising'
findings.truth: Pieterson was among the first killed; Hastings Ndlovu is generally recorded as shot before him. The lesson body already says 'among the first killed', so the definition contradicts the text.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Hector Pieterson'

findings.claim: 'the regime intended to destroy the BCM as it had destroyed the ANC fifteen years earlier'
findings.truth: The ANC was banned in April 1960, seventeen years before the October 1977 bannings, and its leaders were jailed in 1964, thirteen years before. Neither reading gives fifteen.
findings.evidence: dates within this unit

findings.claim: 'South Africa had been expelled from the Commonwealth in 1961' (also in a key fact, a matching question and a flashcard)
findings.truth: South Africa was not expelled. Verwoerd withdrew South Africa's application for continued membership as a republic in March 1961, in the face of attacks on apartheid from other members, and it left on 31 May 1961. The withdraw/expel distinction is a standard precision point.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'South Africa and the Commonwealth of Nations'

findings.claim: 'In 1970 the International Cricket Conference expelled South Africa.'
findings.truth: South Africa's membership had already lapsed in 1961, when leaving the Commonwealth ended its place in what was then the Imperial Cricket Conference. In 1970 its tour of England was called off under government pressure and it was shut out of Test cricket until 1991.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'South Africa national cricket team'; 'International Cricket Council'

findings.claim: 'Examiners notice vague answers like "there were sanctions"'
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: 'Black local councillors appointed under the tricameral system were attacked as collaborators'
findings.truth: The tricameral parliament excluded black South Africans entirely, so it created no black councillors. They were elected, on tiny turnouts, under the Black Local Authorities Act of 1982. Their rent rises triggered the Vaal uprising of September 1984.
findings.evidence: Black Local Authorities Act 1982; spec content on the 1983 constitution

findings.claim: Botha's Rubicon speech 'contributed directly to the Chase Manhattan Bank crisis days later'
findings.truth: The sequence is reversed. A US bank was already threatening to call in its loan while the speech was being drafted; Chase Manhattan had refused to roll the loans over before 15 August 1985. The speech then pushed other banks to follow, the rand collapsed and the government froze debt repayments in September 1985.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Rubicon speech': the bank pressure predates the speech

findings.claim: 'The Inkatha-ANC violence is also examiner material'
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about exam content. Rewritten as revision advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: Cyril Ramaphosa described as 'South Africa's first post-apartheid Deputy President and subsequent President'
findings.truth: The first post-apartheid Deputy Presidents were Thabo Mbeki and F.W. de Klerk. Ramaphosa was ANC Secretary-General and chaired the Constitutional Assembly that wrote the 1996 constitution; he became Deputy President in 2014 and President in 2018.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Cyril Ramaphosa'; 'Government of National Unity (South Africa)'

findings.claim: Revision tip: 'Name two historians or sources with different readings.'
findings.truth: This section of the paper carries no marks for historians' interpretations. Its assessment objectives are recall, second-order concepts and the use of primary sources; interpretations are examined only in the period study. Asking students to memorise historians here sends revision time to something that is not assessed.
findings.evidence: spec assessment tables: no AO4 marks anywhere in the non-British depth study, lines 3092-3208

findings.claim: 'any party winning more than 20 per cent of the vote was entitled to cabinet representation'
findings.truth: Under the interim constitution, any party holding at least 20 seats (5 per cent) could claim cabinet portfolios in proportion, and any party holding at least 80 seats (20 per cent) could name an Executive Deputy President. The 20 per cent figure is the Deputy President threshold, which is why de Klerk qualified. The wrong threshold is repeated in a keyed question and a model answer.
findings.evidence: Interim Constitution of South Africa 1993, sections 84 and 88

findings.claim: 'But examiners also credit answers that note what was NOT achieved'
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: 'The Pondoland revolt in the Transkei homeland saw rural Africans rise against hut tax increases'
findings.truth: Two small slips. In 1960-61 the Transkei was not yet a homeland (self-government came in 1963), and the tax grievance under Bantu Authorities was the general tax rather than the older colonial hut tax. Not worth an edit; the revolt itself and its causes are correctly given.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Pondoland revolt'

findings.claim: Bram Fischer 'died in prison in 1975'
findings.truth: Fischer died on 8 May 1975 at his brother's house in Bloemfontein, still a prisoner, after being moved there with terminal cancer. 'Died in custody' is the accurate phrase, but 'died in prison' is the usual textbook shorthand.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Bram Fischer'

findings.claim: 'By the end of 1977, somewhere between 600 and 700 people had been killed'
findings.truth: The official toll was 176; the Cillie Commission counted 575 deaths in the 1976-77 unrest; estimates run up to 700. The lesson gives only the top of the range, though it does flag that estimates vary. Teaching the official figure against the estimate would also serve the source work this paper rewards.
findings.evidence: Cillie Commission report; Wikipedia 'Soweto uprising'

findings.claim: 'CODESA produced the Interim Constitution, agreed in November 1993'
findings.truth: CODESA II broke down in mid-1992. The interim constitution was agreed on 18 November 1993 by the Multi-Party Negotiating Process at Kempton Park. 'CODESA' as shorthand for the whole negotiation is standard at GCSE.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Negotiations to end apartheid in South Africa'

findings.claim: 'International observers, including former US President Jimmy Carter'
findings.truth: Could not verify. The Wikipedia article on the election names no observers at all, and the WebSearch budget was spent. The UN (UNOMSA), the Commonwealth, the OAU and the EU all observed; Carter's presence is unconfirmed either way, so the claim is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1994 South African general election' lists no observers

findings.claim: Unit-wide: every lesson labels its second 10-marker '10 marks - Explain Two Reasons'
findings.truth: 'Explain two reasons/consequences' is another board's stem wording, but the marks are right and an open 'Explain...' question can properly be answered with two developed reasons, so no student is misled about the paper. Left alone rather than churn nine lessons.
findings.evidence: spec assessment tables: question 6 is 'Explain ...' for 10 marks

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'How long did Mandela remain on the US terrorist watchlist?' (2008)
findings.truth: True, and a good discussion point in the lesson body, but as a flashcard it asks students to memorise a 2008 fact for a paper that stops in 1994. Content, not error.
findings.evidence: spec option title: South Africa 1960-1994

summary: Nine lessons checked; no lesson is clean. The systematic fault is the practice bank: every lesson sets a 4-mark 'Describe two features' and a 5-mark 'Outline', neither of which exists in this paper, so 18 questions were relabelled to genuine forms. Content faults are mostly precision errors a History teacher would mark: South Africa 'expelled' from the Commonwealth, Sisulu called treasurer-general, ten Bantustans from the 1959 Act, a reopened Biko inquest that never happened, the Rubicon speech given as the cause of a bank decision that preceded it, and a 20 per cent cabinet threshold that was really 5 per cent. Four exam tips carried invented examiner claims. One Sharpeville statistic had an invented provenance, though its headline figure of 91 dead is real.
